title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files

reading.body:
This incident shows a general-purpose AI coding and agent tool being used as a component in live offensive cyber operations. The Aurora ransomware operators ran Cursor Agent, which itself calls Claude Sonnet, to carry out hands-on exploitation steps against target organizations. The AI tool was not modified or jailbroken in any way described by the reporting; it was used as designed, directed by operators who understood how to structure its task instructions. The failure is one of dual-use deployment: a legitimate productivity tool provided sufficient capability to assist in network intrusion when placed in the hands of malicious actors.

The operators imposed deliberate constraints on the agent's behavior, prohibiting actions such as DCSync attacks and account lockouts. This shows the attackers treating the AI agent as a controllable instrument, tuning its behavior to avoid forensic noise. The exploitation happened at runtime, inside victim networks, and would not have been visible to the AI tool's developers from the tool's own telemetry alone without active monitoring of how agents were being tasked.

What is not established is whether Cursor or Anthropic had any prior knowledge of this use, or whether any finding of legal liability has been made against any party.

reports.title: Russian-speaking cybercriminals used SpaceX’s Cursor AI tool to hack seven companies
Aurora ransomware targets ESXi, abuses Cursor Agent for exploitation

summary:
# Summary

Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team discovered that the Aurora ransomware group, active since April 2026, has developed a Linux variant targeting ESXi environments. The group operated across multiple countries and ran a data leak site. Researchers found that Aurora operators used Cursor Agent, an AI tool running Claude Sonnet, to conduct hands-on exploitation attacks against ten target organizations between April 8 and May 21, 2026. The ESXi ransomware encrypts virtual machine files using ChaCha20 encryption while keeping the hypervisor bootable so victims can see ransom demands. A custom tool called esxi_finder.py was used to scan for and identify ESXi hosts and vCenter servers within victim networks.

Investigators identified a second cluster of Aurora activity with medium confidence, affecting eight organizations across six countries. This group used different tactics, including exploiting SQL Server commands, privilege escalation, and data exfiltration to self-hosted S3 storage. The research revealed that Aurora operators imposed strict operational restrictions on the AI agent, prohibiting DCSync attacks, account lockouts, and adding new computer objects to domains, suggesting a disciplined approach to avoiding detection and maintaining network stability during attacks.
